newsitem.title: USA: Bill considered to bar U.S. visits by HK lawmakers.
newsitem.headline: Bill considered to bar U.S. visits by HK lawmakers.

text.p: Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms was considering introducing a bill to ban Hong Kong's provisional legislature from visiting the United States after China takes over the British colony on June 30, an aide said on Monday.
The legislation has not been drafted so no details were available. If offered, it would have to be passed by both the Senate and House of Representatives and signed by President Bill Clinton.
Helms, a conservative North Carolina Republican, is a fervent anti-Communist.
Last December, then-U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Winston Lord said after a two-day visit to Hong Kong that the United States opposed moves by China to disband Hong Kong's elected legislature.
"We believe that the disbanding of the elected legislature is both unnecessary and unwise," Lord said on Dec. 5. He resigned from the State Department last week and a replacement has not been named.

China has opposed democratic reforms brought in by British colonial Gov. Chris Patten without its approval, and has vowed to replace the elected legislature with a provisional body when it takes over the territory on June 30.

On Sunday, about 300 hundred pro-democracy activists converged on the headquarters of China's de facto diplomatic mission in Hong Kong to protest Beijing's controversial shadow legislature and its plans to dilute civil liberties when it takes back the colony.
The 60-member chamber gathered across the border in Shenzhen on Saturday to avoid legal challenges to its legitimacy in Hong Kong, where opponents have branded it illegal.

Patten, in a radio address on Sunday, urged provisional legislators, almost half of whom sit on the doomed elected legislature to be replaced by the provisional council upon the handover, to explain themselves to the people of Hong Kong.
"Is Hong Kong going to have the same freedoms after 1997 -- yes or no? If the answer to that question is yes, then why, I repeat, why, do we need to make all these changes?

"And if the answer is no, we are entitled to learn just what is going to be usurped, just how much is going to be taken away, why that's going to happen and how it squares with the international covenants and all the other promises China has made," Patten said.
